subject: Engelska 6
title: Literature and film analysis
sourceSummary: Concepts for analysing plot, characters, theme, setting, narrative perspective and basic film terms.

choices: The main character, often the hero
The villain of a story
A minor character with few lines
The narrator of a story
questions.explanation: The protagonist is the main character, often the one whose goal and conflict drive the plot. The villain is instead called the "antagonist".

questions.opener: Something that makes the reader reconsider the whole story.
choices: The final scene of a film
An unexpected turn in the story that changes the reader's understanding
A secondary storyline
The introduction of a new character
questions.explanation: A "plot twist" is an unexpected turn that changes how the reader or viewer understands what has already happened. It is not just about the final scene or a new character appearing.

questions.prompt: What does "theme" mean in literary analysis?
questions.opener: Distinguish it from "setting", which is something quite different.
choices: The physical location where the story takes place
The order in which events happen
The underlying message or central idea of a work
A summary of the plot
questions.explanation: The theme is the work's underlying message or central idea, for example love, power or identity. The setting, by contrast, is the time and place.

questions.opener: Where and when does the story take place?
choices: The main conflict in the story
The author's opinion of the characters
The moral lesson of the story
The time and place in which a story occurs
questions.explanation: "Setting" is the time and place of the action. The conflict, the moral lesson, and the author's attitude towards the characters are other analytical concepts.

questions.prompt: A story told using "I" and "we", from inside a character's head, uses which narrative perspective?
questions.opener: Which pronoun is at the centre of the storytelling?
choices: Third person omniscient
First person
Second person
Third person limited
questions.explanation: First person perspective uses "I"/"we" and gives access to a single character's thoughts. Third person, whether omniscient or limited, instead uses "he"/"she"/"they".

questions.opener: Think about the root of the word: the same as "photo-" but for moving images.
choices: The written script of a film
The visual style and camera work of a film
The music composed for a film
The actors' performances
questions.explanation: "Cinematography" is about the film's visual language — camera angles, lighting and composition. The script, music and acting are other parts of film production.

questions.prompt:
Read the short passage and identify the narrative perspective, then explain how you know.

"I stood at the edge of the platform, watching the train pull away. She never looked back, and I wondered if she ever would."
questions.opener: Which pronoun dominates the narrative, and whose thoughts do we get access to?
steps: The narrator uses "I" and "I wondered" — a clear sign of first person perspective.
We only get access to the narrator's own thoughts and feelings, not to "she"'s inner life — this confirms that we are locked into a single person's perspective.
If the story had instead followed several characters' thoughts (e.g. also what "she" was thinking), it would have been third person omniscient instead.
Conclusion: first-person narration creates closeness to a character but at the same time limits what the reader can know.

questions.prompt: List key vocabulary for discussing literature and film.
questions.opener: The basic concepts you need to analyse text and film in English.
questions.answer: Plot = the sequence of events · Protagonist = main character · Antagonist = opponent/villain · Theme = underlying message · Setting = time and place · Narrative perspective = the perspective from which the story is told (first person, third person limited, third person omniscient) · Plot twist = unexpected turn · Cinematography = the film's visual style and camera work · Foreshadowing = a hint of what is to come.
